Research/2GO
Geometry-aware search

2GO
Let constraint geometry guide the search.

A quadruped must choose among disconnected footholds; a humanoid must coordinate its body and posture through narrow passages. 2GO uses active constraint geometry to shape how a model-based generative planner refines trajectories and explores alternatives. Its two Gs stand for geometry-aware and generative: geometry becomes part of the reverse update, rather than only a test applied to the final plan.

Read the paperFigures & tablesRun this method

The question

How should a generative planner change both its update direction and its exploration when the feasible region is narrow, disconnected, or posture-dependent?

Demonstrations

How it works

01

Read the active geometry

Task context and violation proxies select active constraints. Their normals describe locally important directions for foothold consistency or body clearance.

02

Shape refinement and exploration

A normal-induced metric shapes the denoising direction, while a regularized tangent filter shapes reverse-process noise. Candidate-sampling randomness and added reverse stochasticity remain distinct.

03

Schedule the reverse transport

An adaptive task-geometry schedule separates transport choice from stochasticity, accommodating DDPM-, DDIM-, and flow-like updates as exploration gives way to refinement.

04

Correct and execute

Optional Convex Feasible Set correction addresses residual violations. A reference governor then adapts a selected plan to the tracking limits of the execution controller.

Results

The paper evaluates both the trajectories a planner returns and the references its execution pipeline can follow. These results cover discrete foothold choices and continuous whole-body clearance; planning success and execution success are reported separately.

Harder stepping stones · planning success
88%

S2 pSSR: 2GO 88%, MDOC 68%, MD-COAS 14%, MBD 4%, MPPI 20%. Five seeds, ten returned trajectories per seed; goal tolerance 0.20 m.

Stepping stones · planning to execution
98% / 80%

S1: 98% planning pSSR and 80% governed MuJoCo Go2 eSSR. Execution selects and adapts one reference per seed, across five trials; the two percentages measure different populations.

Experimental protocol and metric definitions

Five seeds, with ten clean trajectories per seed. pV and pT are mean ± population standard deviation over the five seed-level values.

The main comparison uses a 48 GB NVIDIA RTX A6000 and nine CPU cores. Planning time covers the complete multi-candidate solve and excludes later execution screening, margin calibration, and deployment.

Nominal sampling/update budgets: 512 samples for stepping stones, 1024 for corridors, and 100 optimizer or reverse steps. These counts do not imply equal wall-clock cost.

pV is mean foothold distance in centimeters for the selected planning candidate.

Quadruped eSSR measures the assisted MuJoCo execution model: the common follower constructs gait and footholds and includes supplementary floating-base PD stabilization.

Experimental protocol and metric definitions

Five seeds, with ten clean trajectories per seed. pV and pT are mean ± population standard deviation over the five seed-level values.

The main comparison uses a 48 GB NVIDIA RTX A6000 and nine CPU cores. Planning time covers the complete multi-candidate solve and excludes later execution screening, margin calibration, and deployment.

Nominal sampling/update budgets: 512 samples for stepping stones, 1024 for corridors, and 100 optimizer or reverse steps. These counts do not imply equal wall-clock cost.

pV is sampled obstacle-band occupancy (%), distinct from the body-proxy clearance test used by pSSR.

eSSR measures the reported selection-and-adaptation pipelines, including their differences. Humanoid 2GO additionally uses simulated execution screening and clearance-margin calibration.

Execution requires reaching the fixed task goal within 0.20 m, no fall, and nonnegative modeled body-proxy clearance. Real-world G1 AR demonstrations are qualitative and are not included in this simulation table.

Scope & trade-offs

Evaluated on quadruped stepping stones and humanoid corridors, with planning metrics separated from governed MuJoCo execution. The hardware demonstration uses a real Unitree G1 with motion-capture-registered AR obstacles and the built-in locomotion controller. It is qualitative deployment evidence with virtual obstacles.

Performance depends on the task: in the U-shaped corridor, 2GO achieves 48% pSSR versus 90% for MDOC. The progression across these papers does not imply uniform dominance.

Planning and governed execution use different evaluation criteria. Candidate selection and controller adaptation can change outcomes; execution percentages should not be read as planner-only effects.

The real G1 video demonstrates navigation relative to AR obstacles. It does not establish a real-world success rate against physical walls.

The next question

MD-COAS adapts how feasibility is enforced during generation. 2GO asks how local constraint geometry should also shape the direction and randomness of that process. MGA subsequently investigates contact-responsive motion–impedance control, where feasible commands must be reconsidered through their physical realization.

Figures and tables reproduce the manuscript's reported experiments. Demonstrations are representative runs; experimental populations and metrics are specified with each table.
